```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE)
```

**QuickMap makes making gorgeous, interesting air quality maps easy.** Maps are **ready in minutes for publication or to put on a website.** Quickmap is **designed for UK council air quality officers**, so it uses the kind of data you already have, like the Excel tables you use for an ASR. It can also pull in data from a live data source like Breathe London API, or the Defra AURN data provided through [OpenAir](https://openair-project.github.io/book/) data pull. 

The **map images are print quality**, suitable to include in an AQAP, newsletter or local report.

The **web maps are self-contained files**, so you can email them or put them on a website. Compact, fast animations are easy to create, so they can be emailed emailed to a colleague, a local interest group or a councillor to show them what's been going on.

This page takes you through two fully worked examples - they might be all you ever need to know. **Make a nice report map** shows you how to make a perfect map for a report or publication, one step at a time, from importing some data, through to choosing the colour scheme, adjusting the various titles, overlaying school locations, and so on.

**Make an animated map** takes you further, creating an animated map you can put on a website, or a GIF. The animated map lets you zoom, show the actual values, and loop over time. The maps shown are real QuickMap output — click, drag and play with them. Along the way, each step points to the chapter that takes that feature further.

## 1. Install

Install from GitHub:

```{r install, purl = FALSE}
# install.packages("devtools")            # if you don't have it
devtools::install_github("ngnrfsk/quickmap")
```

> The repository is public, so no GitHub token is needed. A CRAN release
> is planned, after which `install.packages("quickmap")` will do.

# Basics - customise nice report maps

One dataset (a Wandsworth diffusion tube survey), one map, growing by one
line per step.

## 2. Make your first map — two arguments

```{r first-map, purl = FALSE}
library(quickmap)                           # load the quickmap library
quickmap(
  "~/my_data/tubes_wandsworth.csv", # diffusion tube data
  output_file = "wandsworth.html"   # where to write the map
)
```

Two things — the measurement data, and where to put the result — are all
`quickmap()` needs. It never picks the location for you: a bare name like
`"wandsworth.html"` goes in your working directory, a path such as
`"maps/wandsworth.html"` goes there and creates the folder. The data here
is an ordinary diffusion tube spreadsheet saved as CSV:

| Easting | Northing | 2017 | 2018 | ... | 2024 | Label |
|---------|----------|------|------|-----|------|-------|
| 528900  | 172431   | 33   | 31   | ... | 15.9 | 11b Elmbourne Road |
| 530129  | 177727   |      | 49   | ... | 22.9 | 1 Nine Elms |

*Minimum required: `Easting`, `Northing` and at least one year column.
Anything else is optional. (Full input specifications: the* Your data
*chapter.)*

QuickMap converts the coordinates, colours each site by the WHO NO2
bands, fits the view to the data, and writes `wandsworth.html` —
a single self-contained file. Open it in any browser, attach it to an
email, or put it on a website (it does need an internet connection to
download the background map). Here is that exact file:

<iframe src="https://ngnrfsk.github.io/quickmap/articles/maps/getstarted-first.html" width="100%" height="440" loading="lazy" style="border:1px solid #ddd; border-radius:6px;" title="First map: Wandsworth diffusion tubes, no boundary"></iframe>

**Reading the map:**

- **Symbols** are monitoring sites, coloured by pollution level — green
  is good, red is bad. Labels can be added that appear on hover — step 8.
- **The legend** (along the bottom) names each colour band. The bands
  come from a colour scale (`who_no2` by default) — swap it with
  `colour_scale =`, as Part 2 does. Click the legend header to collapse it.
- **The time slider** (bottom of the map) appears because your CSV had
  several year columns. Drag it, step with ‹ ›, or press play to animate.
- **The banner** (top) is the map's title — customised in step 7.

## 3. Draw a borough boundary

Air quality reporting is usually about a place; naming it draws its
boundary and frames the map around it:

```{r boundary, purl = FALSE}
quickmap(
  "~/my_data/tubes_wandsworth.csv",
  boroughs    = "Wandsworth",               # NEW: the boundary to draw
  output_file = "wandsworth.html"
)
```

**More on boundaries:**

- `boroughs` takes one name, several (`c("Wandsworth", "Richmond")`), or
  `"All"` for every London borough.
- The area's name can be written on the map with
  `boundary_labels = TRUE` — useful on multi-borough maps.
- The boundary also drives the next step's vignette and the map's
  framing.

<iframe src="https://ngnrfsk.github.io/quickmap/articles/maps/getstarted-boundary.html" width="100%" height="440" loading="lazy" style="border:1px solid #ddd; border-radius:6px;" title="The same map with the Wandsworth boundary and vignette"></iframe>

## 4. The vignette — focus attention inside the boundary

The map above dims everything outside Wandsworth. That is the
**vignette**, on by default whenever a boundary is drawn, so the reader's
eye goes to the area the map is about. Written out explicitly:

```{r vignette, purl = FALSE}
quickmap(
  "~/my_data/tubes_wandsworth.csv",
  boroughs    = "Wandsworth",
  vignette    = TRUE,                       # NEW: dim outside the boundary
  output_file = "wandsworth.html"           #      (the default with a boundary)
)
```

<iframe src="https://ngnrfsk.github.io/quickmap/articles/maps/getstarted-boundary.html" width="100%" height="440" loading="lazy" style="border:1px solid #ddd; border-radius:6px;" title="Vignette on: dimmed outside the boundary"></iframe>

Set `vignette = FALSE` to show the surroundings at full brightness:

<iframe src="https://ngnrfsk.github.io/quickmap/articles/maps/getstarted-vignette-off.html" width="100%" height="440" loading="lazy" style="border:1px solid #ddd; border-radius:6px;" title="Vignette off: full brightness everywhere"></iframe>

*The vignette's colour follows the map's theme — themes bundle all such
choices into one reusable YAML file (`?load_theme`).*

## 5. Save typing: tell QuickMap where your data lives

Optional, but worth doing once: if your data files sit in one folder, set
`DATA_PATH` and use bare filenames everywhere (the rest of this page
assumes it is set):

```{r datapath, purl = FALSE}
Sys.setenv(
  DATA_PATH = "~/my_data"                  # folder where your data lives
)
quickmap(
  "tubes_wandsworth.csv",          # NEW: just the filename
  boroughs    = "Wandsworth",
  output_file = "wandsworth.html"
)
```

## 6. Export a static map for a report

Documents need still images. `export_image` writes a JPG next to the
HTML, at any size — text and legend scale with the image:

```{r export}
library(quickmap)                          # (already loaded if you followed above)
quickmap(
  "tubes_wandsworth.csv",
  boroughs      = "Wandsworth",
  display_times = "2024",                  # NEW: one year -> one image
  export_image  = c(1200, 900),            # NEW: JPG width x height, pixels
  output_file   = "wandsworth.html"        #      the JPG goes beside it
)
```

![The exported JPG: 1200×900, ready for a report](https://ngnrfsk.github.io/quickmap/articles/maps/getstarted-export.jpg)

*With several time steps selected you get one JPG per step;
`export_image = TRUE` uses the default 1200×1200. `display_times` also
subsets interactive maps — pick any years, months or hours present in
the data.*

## 7. Add a title, and put the file where you want it

Maps usually need a title for the banner, and a file name you'll
recognise later. `output_dir` sets the folder once, so the file names
stay short:

```{r step-further}
quickmap(
  "tubes_wandsworth.csv",
  boroughs    = "Wandsworth",
  title       = "Wandsworth NO2, 2017-2024", # NEW: banner text
  output_file = "wandsworth_no2.html",       # NEW: a name you'll recognise
  output_dir  = "aq_maps"                    # NEW: the folder to write into
)
```

*`output_dir` is created if it does not exist. To use one folder for a
whole session, set `options(quickmap.output_dir = "aq_maps")` — in
`.Rprofile` if you always want it — and drop the argument.*

<iframe src="https://ngnrfsk.github.io/quickmap/articles/maps/getstarted-titled.html" width="100%" height="440" loading="lazy" style="border:1px solid #ddd; border-radius:6px;" title="The map with its banner title"></iframe>

*The accent colour under the title can be set directly with
`banner_colour =`; the banner's style (white strip or colour bar) and
the full colour scheme are theme settings (`?load_theme`).*

## 8. Add labels to the symbols

Readers often want the number behind a colour. `symbol_labels = TRUE`
shows each site's value when you hover over its symbol — try it on the
map below:

```{r labels}
quickmap(
  "tubes_wandsworth.csv",
  boroughs      = "Wandsworth",
  title         = "Wandsworth NO2, 2017-2024",
  symbol_labels = TRUE,                      # NEW: values appear on hover
  output_file   = "wandsworth_no2.html",
  output_dir    = "aq_maps"
)
```

<iframe src="https://ngnrfsk.github.io/quickmap/articles/maps/getstarted-labels.html" width="100%" height="440" loading="lazy" style="border:1px solid #ddd; border-radius:6px;" title="Hover a symbol to see its value"></iframe>

*Labels have five modes — off, values on hover, values always shown, and
site names (from a `Label` or `School` column) on hover or always shown:
`symbol_labels = "values_on"`, `"labels"`, `"labels_on"` (`?quickmap`).*

## 9. Combine several measurement networks

Different monitoring networks — and context like schools — go on one map
by listing the files. Each network keeps its own symbol, and putting the
symbols in the title turns the banner into a key:

```{r networks}
quickmap(
  list(
    "tubes_merton.csv",                             # diffusion tubes
    "sensors_london.RData", # sensor network
    "schools_merton.csv"                                   # school locations
  ),
  boroughs = "Merton",
  title = "Merton NO2: ● tubes ◆ sensors ✖ schools", # NEW: symbols as a key
  output_file = "merton_no2.html",
  output_dir = "aq_maps"
)
```

<iframe src="https://ngnrfsk.github.io/quickmap/articles/maps/getstarted-networks.html" width="100%" height="440" loading="lazy" style="border:1px solid #ddd; border-radius:6px;" title="Three networks on one map, symbols keyed in the banner"></iframe>

*Naming layers, choosing each network's pollutant or symbol
(`data_symbols`, `qm_layer()`), and mapping data frames you built
yourself: the [Layers](layers.html) chapter — start at "Use the `layers`
list to add sources".*

# Part 2 — Build an animation

A new dataset (five days of hourly sensor readings during a January 2024
pollution episode), and two steps. These maps keep the default
OpenStreetMap background; for dense data a paler background can suit
better — switching is one theme line
(`map: base_tiles: "CartoDB.Positron"`, `?load_theme`).

## 10. Animate a pollution episode

This maps 108 hourly time steps and starts playing by itself — pause it
with the round button, drag the slider to any hour, or change the pace
with the multiplier button at the right of the card:

```{r animation}
quickmap(
  from_rdata("episode_london.RData", # hourly sensor export
             "pm25",                              # pollutant to map
             name = "Sensors"),                   # layer name for the map
  boroughs     = c("Wandsworth", "Richmond"),     # two boundaries
  colour_scale = "stripes_pm25",                  # a PM2.5 colour scale
  title        = "PM2.5 Episode: Jan 15-20, 2024",
  output_file  = "episode.html",
  autoplay     = TRUE,                            # play on open
  play_speed   = 500                              # ms per hour; omit to
)                                                 # let the step count decide
```

<iframe src="https://ngnrfsk.github.io/quickmap/articles/maps/getstarted-episode.html" width="100%" height="480" loading="lazy" style="border:1px solid #ddd; border-radius:6px;" title="108-step hourly animation"></iframe>

Above 50 time steps QuickMap automatically switches to a compact storage
format, so even this five-day hourly animation stays around 1 MB — small
enough to email. *Colour scales for other pollutants and boroughs:
`?load_colour_scale`.*

## 11. Add live wind to the animation

Where did the pollution come from? An animated wind-particle overlay
answers that at a glance. `from_worldmet()` fetches real weather-station
data (here Heathrow) from NOAA, and the particles advance with the time
slider:

```{r net-wind}
heathrow <- from_worldmet(station = "037720-99999", # Heathrow station id
                          year = 2024)              # fetches from NOAA
quickmap(
  from_rdata("episode_london.RData", "pm25", name = "Sensors"),
  boroughs     = c("Wandsworth", "Richmond"),
  colour_scale = "stripes_pm25",
  title        = "PM2.5 Episode with wind: Jan 15-20, 2024",
  output_file  = "episode_wind.html",
  autoplay     = TRUE,
  play_speed   = 500,
  wind         = heathrow                           # NEW: the wind overlay
)
```

<iframe src="https://ngnrfsk.github.io/quickmap/articles/maps/getstarted-wind.html" width="100%" height="480" loading="lazy" style="border:1px solid #ddd; border-radius:6px;" title="The animation with a live wind-particle overlay"></iframe>

Wind particles are coloured by wind speed. *Requires the `worldmet`
package and an internet connection for the NOAA fetch; particle styling
and station choice: the* Wind *chapter.*
